what_it_does: Modern computer memory chips (DRAM) store data in rows of cells that are physically close together. A well-known attack called RowHammer repeatedly reads from one row so often that it disturbs neighboring rows, potentially flipping bits and letting an attacker corrupt another program's memory or escape a security boundary. Hardware fixes are expensive and slow to ship, and software workarounds have been repeatedly defeated. Citadel is a smarter software memory allocator — the part of the operating system that decides which memory locations to hand out to each program — that prevents these cross-program attacks by physically separating every security domain into its own isolated region of DRAM, with guard rows between them so no two domains ever sit adjacent. According to the abstract, this approach incurs only about 7% extra memory use and no noticeable slowdown, and it works on existing hardware without any chip changes.
